title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents
why: A frozen tool-using spatial agent improves orchestration across tasks without parameter updates by retaining two external stores: Experiences (condition-action tactics distilled from contrasting rollouts of the same task) and Skills (multi-step procedures with activation and termination conditions). Experiences can be anchored to an active Skill, scored with a Contrastive Utility Score that withholds them across rollouts, and consolidated into the Skills they support—an A-class retained skill/experience loop for tool orchestration.
mechanism: External Experiences and Skills are updated from the frozen agent's own interaction history. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's contribution by randomly withholding it on repeated rollouts of the same task; consistently useful Experiences are consolidated into the Skills they support, and Experiences may appear only while a Skill is active rather than once per task.
evaluation_signal: Authors report results across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones (20 settings), stating that SpatialCraft achieves the best accuracy in all 20 and that a frozen agent can learn to orchestrate spatial tools from its own experience. These figures are author-reported from the abstract; PDF tables were not opened.

title: AGL-SKILL: Coding Harnesses as Agentic Optimizers
why: Treats textual skills (reusable workflows, code, and prompts) as an editable non-weight surface and shows a coding agent, given a metric, can iteratively refine those skills—and thereby its own task-specific context—outperforming published score-driven skill-optimization methods. Directly in scope as agentic optimization of retained skills inside a coding harness.
mechanism: A coding agent acts as the optimizer for skill artifacts (workflows, code, and prompts) through iterative, metric-guided edits, as an alternative to handcrafting, one-shot generation, or score-driven search.
evaluation_signal: Authors report that, across five benchmarks, a coding agent without guidance substantially improves every target and outperforms published skill-optimization methods. These comparisons are author-reported from the abstract; the five benchmark names and tables were not opened in the PDF.

title: VISE: Verifier-Independent Skill Self-Evolution with Feedback from Tool Implementations
why: Proposes verifier-independent skill self-evolution: skill workflows are revised by comparing current instructions with capabilities, inputs, conditions, and output formats extracted from tool source code, plus the task request and execution trace, then recommending edits linked to those implementations. This is a retained skill-evolution method that does not depend on a task-specific verifier.
mechanism: VISE is added as a scripts-first revision stage. It extracts tool capabilities and usage conditions from source, diffs them against current workflow instructions using the request and execution trace, and proposes specific skill edits tied to the relevant implementation and conditions.
evaluation_signal: Authors report VISE as an additional revision stage for four evolution methods on SkillsBench and SkillLearnBench: versus the corresponding no-verifier conditions, overall average task success rises by 9.14–13.35 percentage points, and the share of tasks solved in all three runs rises by 12.36–18.29 points. A case study is said to show how revised instructions connect tool outputs to later steps. Figures are author-reported from the abstract.

title: RecurSciBench: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement in Data-Driven Scientific Research
why: A scalable RSI benchmark for data-driven scientific research. RecurSciPipe builds executable, scientifically verified modeling and analysis tasks from raw datasets, then evaluates whether self-improvement on source tasks transfers to independent tasks (within-type, cross-type, and cross-domain). In scope as an audit/benchmark of self-improving agents, including reported regressions.
mechanism: The resource is a benchmark and construction pipeline (RecurSciPipe) with execution-based and scientific-validity checks. Evaluation compares each RSI system's initial and evolved states on independent tasks after evolution on source tasks, covering within-type, cross-type, and cross-domain transfer.
evaluation_signal: Authors report evaluating four RSI systems across four scientific domains, multiple data modalities, and varied objectives. They state that self-improvement benefits vary by system and domain, that positive overall gains can coexist with per-task regressions, and that experience can transfer across task types and even benefit other domains without measurable source-domain gains. Details are author-reported from the abstract; per-system tables were not opened.

title: MetaFORGE: A Meta-Learning Framework for Harness Optimization in Automated Code Generation for Parallel Computing
why: Iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation with textual-gradient refinement driven by a scalar reward from correctness tests, compiler diagnostics, static analysis, runtime, and load-imbalance profiles, plus an external memory that distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments are described as evidence that optimization knowledge persists in the transferred skill and the memory—an A-class retained skill/memory loop, not weight updates.
mechanism: Execution-grounded meta-learning updates persistent NL skill specs via textual-gradient refinement. An external memory stores and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. The skill and memory are the retained non-weight artifacts.
evaluation_signal: Authors report results on six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, with improvements in static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance versus zero-shot generation, generally exceeding a TextGrad iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation (refinement model reduced to gpt-4o) and an expanded retrieval ablation over all 18 task–workload configurations are described, plus leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments for persistence of skill and memory. Figures are author-reported from the abstract.

title: Failure Broadens, Success Sharpens: Continual Adaptation of Tool-Use Agents Across Diverse Tasks with Dual-Polarity Memory
why: A retrieval-free procedural-memory workflow (DualPM) lets tool-use agents self-improve over heterogeneous task streams by writing reflection and procedural memory from both local successes and failures, then periodically consolidating under a capacity limit. This is a retained memory/playbook component for continual adaptation, with an external check on EvoMemBench.
mechanism: Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance generates customizable reflection and procedural memory from successes and failures within each trajectory, then periodically consolidates memory under a fixed capacity so the store does not explode over long streams. The workflow is retrieval-free.
evaluation_signal: Authors report online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics: failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, and combining both polarities integrates the two effects. Further studies are said to show cross-domain generalization and continual adaptation, and external evaluation on EvoMemBench is reported as evidence of portability. Comments state acceptance at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Towards Test-Time Continual Learning Agents. Figures are author-reported from the abstract.

title: TransHarness: From Benchmark Overfitting to Transferable Harness Evolution
why: Evolves coding-agent harness intervention policies from same-task success–failure contrasts without updating model weights, then uses cross-task replay and independent semantic selection so retained policies transfer beyond the evolution benchmark. Directly addresses a known failure mode of harness evolution (overfitting the evolution set).
mechanism: TransHarness derives harness intervention policies that couple execution-context triggers with diagnostic guidance. Cross-task replay and independent semantic selection keep policies that intervene selectively and ground corrections in current-task evidence. An independent evolution set is curated for cross-distribution transfer.
evaluation_signal: Authors report a cross-benchmark evaluation over multiple models and lightweight and mature harnesses. With only 300 source trajectories from outside the test distribution, TransHarness is said to further improve strong agents on distinct target benchmarks, with author-reported scores of 76.4% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 95.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 2.4 and 5.6 points above the strongest baseline model (GPT-6 Astra). Figures are author-reported from the abstract.

title: EGSE: Evidence-Grounded Skill Evolution for Medical Reasoning Agents
why: Distills historical dialogues from similar cases into reusable conditional workflows and progressively refines a multi-faceted skill library through source-grounded review and execution validation. Experiences are extracted by contrasting successful and failed rollouts and synthesized into workflows whose checks are traceable to source dialogues—an A-class retained skill-evolution loop for medical agents.
mechanism: EGSE evaluates intermediate reasoning and tool use, contrasts repeated successful and failed rollouts, and synthesizes experiences into workflows with applicability conditions and source-traceable checks. Library additions and merges require source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference, queries are routed to skill nodes (modality, task type, disease) and applicable workflows are selected from their conditions.
evaluation_signal: Authors report that across four chest X-ray benchmarks, EGSE outperforms representative medical agents and skill-evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls, with consistent accuracy gains across seven foundation models and support for skill transfer across datasets. Figures are author-reported from the abstract; PDF tables were not opened.

title: MedSkill-E$^{2}$: Evaluating and Evolving Skills for Medical Agents
why: Documents skill Enable But Underuse (EBU)—agents have a skill's rules but fail to apply them autonomously—then evolves reusable skill instructions from execution feedback comparing autonomous versus explicitly guided skill use. EBU-Bench and EBU-Evolve form a B/A pair: an audit of skill use across model-harness combinations, plus retained skill revisions that transfer across models and harnesses.
mechanism: EBU-Evolve uses execution feedback from autonomous and explicitly guided skill use to distill effective guidance into reusable skill instructions. The evolved skills are the retained artifact. EBU-Bench covers 12 medically relevant task groups and associated skills and quantifies the EBU gap as the difference in skill-use accuracy between autonomous use and guided reading/application of the same skill.
evaluation_signal: Authors report that on EBU-Bench every evaluated model-harness combination exhibits EBU, with a mean gap of 43.94 percentage points, and that for a fixed model, autonomous skill-use accuracy differs by up to 38.96 points across harnesses. Relative to pre-evolution versions, revised skills are said to improve autonomous skill-use accuracy by 33.33 to 55.17 points and to keep helping when transferred across multiple models and harnesses, including on unseen tasks within the same skill. Figures are author-reported from the abstract.

title: EvoLink-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Interdependent Task Streams
why: A benchmark for self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams (office work, multi-turn dialogue, AutoResearch-style workflows) with persistent workspaces. It separates L1 language-expressible knowledge revision from L2 task-level capability development, and scores within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse on later dependent tasks—including negative findings that persistence does not necessarily help later tasks.
mechanism: The resource is a streaming benchmark with two levels (L1 knowledge acquisition/revision; L2 capability development via execution and feedback) and an evaluation that distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and later-task experience reuse. Agents are compared under three persistence conditions.
evaluation_signal: Authors report evaluating five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations and three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. They state that no framework is consistently best on both levels, retries recover only a limited share of failed tasks, persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance, and evolution effects differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks and across domains. Figures are author-reported from the abstract.

title: HoMe: Toward Practical Harness Optimization of Memory Systems for AI Assistants
why: An evaluation-driven loop that iteratively edits the full memory-system harness (code, prompts, and configurations for construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation) rather than only model weights. Candidate harnesses are derived from previously evaluated ones, with session-level memory versioning and traces used to localize shared failure mechanisms to harness components—an A-class retained harness-optimization method for assistant memory.
mechanism: HoMe evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate by editing any part of a previously evaluated harness. Session-level memory versioning plus execution traces identify shared failure mechanisms and localize them to sessions and harness components. Candidate gating, smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and reuse of constructed memory are used to explore structure early and cut evaluation cost.
evaluation_signal: Authors report validation with the open-source memory system ReMe on LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark after a full initial evaluation, HoMe is said to discover harnesses that improve end-task performance over the original strong harness while using far fewer query-time tokens. Figures are author-reported from the abstract.

title: PRECEPT: Security Self-Improvement of Coding Agents via Evolving Principles
why: Defines security self-improvement as retaining lessons from an agent's own security failures across sessions. PRECEPT starts from authoritative secure-coding principles and revises a principle library against those failures so principles fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong; a revision is kept only if fresh executions are more secure while functional success stays within a tolerance of the unaided agent. In scope as a retained, evaluated principle/playbook loop (not a one-shot prompt).
mechanism: An evolving library begins from published secure-coding principles and is revised from the agent's own security-repair failures. A candidate revision is retained only if new executions show more secure code while functional success stays within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement is described as continuing across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first.
evaluation_signal: Authors first report that, across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same class in a new session 26.7% of the time (versus 27.5% for agents that had never seen it); neither persistent context of the repair nor published principles closed the gap. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent is reported at 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%. Figures are author-reported from the abstract.
